title: VPN
summary: A virtual private network establishes an encrypted tunnel between endpoints or gateways so that traffic crossing an untrusted network cannot be read or modified in transit, and so that the endpoints can be treated as members of a logical private network. Site-to-site tunnels join branch offices or cloud networks using IPsec or comparable protocols, while remote-access VPNs connect individual users through a concentrator that authenticates them and places them on an internal subnet. The security properties come from the cryptographic handshake, mutual authentication of peers, and integrity protection of each packet, but the trust model is the weak point. A remote-access VPN that grants full internal reachability reproduces the flat network for every connected device, so a compromised laptop inherits the same access as a workstation on site. Split tunnelling compounds the problem by allowing the endpoint to talk directly to the internet while holding an internal tunnel, which turns the endpoint into a bridge between the two. Operationally, VPN concentrators concentrate risk. They are internet-facing, they authenticate users, and they are frequently targeted by credential stuffing, password spraying and exploitation of unpatched appliances, so they must be patched aggressively, protected with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, and monitored for unusual session behaviour such as logins from unexpected geographies or impossible travel. Capacity planning matters because a saturated concentrator becomes an availability incident. Many organisations are reducing reliance on broad network-level access in favour of application-level access brokers that authorise a specific service rather than placing a device on the internal network. Where VPNs remain, good practice includes per-user authorisation profiles, session timeouts, device posture checks before access is granted, and complete logging of tunnel establishment and termination.
objectives: You will be able to explain what a VPN does and does not protect once a device is connected.
You will be able to compare site-to-site and remote-access designs and their trust assumptions.
You will be able to assess split tunnelling and full tunnelling against endpoint risk.
You will be able to triage VPN authentication logs for spraying, stuffing and anomalous session behaviour.
You will be able to harden a concentrator with multi-factor authentication, patching discipline and per-user profiles.
You will be able to justify moving sensitive access from network-level tunnels to application-level brokers.
